analysis: Interpretation, not graph proof. The three questions share a surface (the Gate Table) but not obviously one problem. q-gate-table asks an existence question about the world: is the Hollow Gate and Gate Table accepted, and may the Council pass through it. q-reform-stance asks a thematic-stance question: does the Table model reform from within or warn against it. q-plurality asks an end-state question: does any terrace keep a measured ledger in Book 30, and is plurality the intended ending. By narrative function the Table is a coordination device. By causal role it sits between two recorded practices (the counted Turn and the gift practice) that both depend on one outlet, and between the Council and a body that holds no record. By reader effect it carries the cost of counting and the hope that a shared practice outlives its institution. Read as one mechanism, the recorded structure supports a link. The Gate is where plurality is made mechanically necessary, since the counted practice needs water held back and the gift practice needs release at need. The Table is the valley's answer to that, formed in Book 22 and taking the schedule from the Council. Whether that answer counts as reform from within depends on a fact the candidate leaves open. That fact is whether the Table is the Council changing itself, or a new body the Council has to accept. The Council's schedule-setting is the object of the Book 21 conflict, and the Council is the institution that would be reformed. So the stance question can only be read through the Table if the Table's relation to the Council is settled, and that is exactly what q-gate-table's revision (may the Council pass through it) is asking. Reading the three as one problem, with the Table as a single mechanism, would make a coherent thematic spine. Plurality would be what the Table preserves, and reform from within would be how the Council arrives at the Table. It would cost the Series the chance for the Table to fail. The candidate's own risk note says the Table may become a seat of power, and Alternative B names the Hall's custody returning under another name. A Table that is both the stance's proof and the plurality's guarantee has no room for that failure, and would be easy to read as the author's endorsement. Reading the Table as warning against one of them pulls the questions apart. It could warn against reform from within (the Hall was broken in Book 5, not reformed, and the Table is a new body), which keeps plurality but makes the Council's passage through the Gate look like capture rather than change. Or it could warn against plurality (permanent plural practice at one gate keeps producing a body with power over the schedule), which would make a measured ledger in Book 30 a liability instead of an end state. That reading is sharper and more tragic, but it costs the hope the candidate already commits to (et_hope, rx_hope), where a shared practice outlasts its institution. The questions should therefore stay partly independent. q-gate-table should be settled first, because it fixes what the Table is and whether the Council can pass through it, and the other two inherit different readings from it. q-reform-stance and q-plurality are about different things: a stance about institutions, and an end state about practices. Plurality at Book 30 does not require reform from within (a measured terrace can persist beside the gift practice whether the Council reformed or was displaced), and reform from within does not require plurality (a reformed Council might still absorb one practice). They are coupled only through the Table, not through each other. The author may decide they are one problem, but the candidate does not record that coupling, so treat the link as a hypothesis to test rather than a shared problem already present in the graph.

recorded_observations.claim: The working candidate records, as undecided, whether reform from within remains the series' stance and whether the Gate Table models it or warns against it.
The working candidate records, as undecided, whether any terrace keeps a measured ledger in Book 30 and whether plurality of practice is the intended end state.

The working candidate records, as undecided, whether the Hollow Gate and Gate Table are accepted parts of the world (both are construction additions), revised to ask whether the Council may pass through it.

The candidate records the Hollow Gate as the sluice dividing the high cistern's release between upper and lower channels; the Council has set its schedule since the Turn, and the schedule is the object of the Book 21 conflict.

The candidate records that the counted practice holds water back to protect the high cistern, while the gift practice needs release at need (l_unmeasured_needs_release), both resting on the same Gate.
The candidate records that the Terrace Council sets the Hollow Gate schedule until the Gate Table takes it in Book 22.
The candidate records that two proven practices at one Gate force the question of whose practice sets the schedule, with the stated risk that the Gate Table becomes a seat of power.
The candidate records the Table as a rotating body that sets the schedule and holds no record, formed in answer to two proven practices contesting one outlet.

hypotheses.title: One mechanism: the Table preserves plurality and is how reform arrives
hypotheses.description: Interpretive reading: the Table is a single device in which the Council cedes the schedule while both practices survive. Reform from within is the route and plurality is the result. This would give the Series a single thematic spine and let Book 30 echo Book 22. It would cost the Table the capacity to fail, and risks reading as author endorsement.

hypotheses.title: The Table warns against reform from within
hypotheses.description: Interpretive reading: the Council could not hold both practices, so the valley made a new body. Plurality survives because the incumbent was displaced rather than reformed, which is consistent with the Hall's break in Book 5. This keeps the plurality question open but makes any Council passage through the Gate look like capture, and it answers q-reform-stance negatively without deciding q-plurality.

hypotheses.title: The Table warns against plurality
hypotheses.description: Interpretive reading: permanent plural practice at one shared gate keeps producing a body with power over the schedule, so a measured ledger in Book 30 is a standing cost, not a settled end state. This is darker and sharper, and it would put pressure on the hope the candidate commits to (et_hope, rx_hope), where a shared practice outlasts its institution.

hypotheses.title: Independent questions joined only through the Table
hypotheses.description: Interpretive reading: q-gate-table is a world-acceptance decision that fixes what the Table is. q-reform-stance (a stance about institutions) and q-plurality (an end state about practices) can each be answered without the other. This keeps each answer cheap to revise, at the cost of a thinner thematic link between Books 22 and 30.

uncertainties: The candidate does not record whether the Gate Table is the Council changing itself or a separate body the Council must accept, and this decides whether reform from within is even a coherent reading of it.

The meaning of the revision 'whether the Council may pass through it' is ambiguous between the Council passing through the Gate physically, taking a seat at the Table, or being subject to its schedule.
The Hollow Gate and Gate Table are agent-proposed construction additions, so an author who rejects them removes the shared anchor and the three questions would no longer share a subject.
The candidate does not record any relation linking q-reform-stance and q-plurality, so any shared creative problem is an interpretation.

The ledger now records hours worked beside each mark, so a measured count could be read from it. The candidate does not say whether a terrace keeping that ledger in Book 30 counts as plurality or as a return of the counted regime.

Finale Alternatives A, B and C each shape the Table differently (no record authority, lot-drawn seats with a sunset, or a ratified trigger), and none is chosen, so the Table's final form is undetermined.
It is not recorded whether the Series is meant to take a stance on reform at all, or whether the Table is only a mechanism that leaves the stance to the reader.
Which reading of the Table the author prefers is unknown; nothing here attributes a preference to the author.
